notes: Historic child sex abuse conviction appeal; recent fabrication and summing-up grounds are clearly resolved in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Recent fabrication evidence in historic child abuse conviction appeal
key_facts: BL was convicted at St Albans Crown Court of four counts of indecent assault and two counts of indecency with a child against his granddaughter JD, alleged to have occurred when she was aged 7 to 13.
The complainant reported the greenhouse incidents to her mother AP when aged 13 or 14; contact with the appellant ceased in 1977 or 1978 and she went to the police in 2002.
The judge admitted AP's evidence as rebutting recent fabrication after cross-examination suggesting the allegations were made up in the 1980s or later.
The appellant, aged 83 with serious medical conditions, was originally sentenced to five years on the indecent assault counts and two years on the indecency counts, all concurrent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence by leave of the single judge to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed as safe; sentence appeal allowed in part with five-year terms reduced to 2½ years on indecent assault counts and 18 months on indecency counts, all concurrent.
enrichment.ratio: Where cross-examination and police interview material invited the inference that no complaint was made until long after contact ceased, evidence of a complaint to the complainant's mother in 1977 was admissible as rebutting recent fabrication; once admitted, the judge's directions sufficiently limited the jury's use of that evidence, though an express direction that it could not prove truth would have been preferable.
legal_issues: Whether the mother's evidence was properly admitted as rebutting recent fabrication
Whether the trial judge adequately directed the jury on the limited use of complaint evidence
Whether the total sentence was manifestly excessive given the appellant's age and ill-health

notes: Pure economic loss duty of care in police transfer context; Hedley Byrne analysis is detailed and outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Police officer's claim for lost housing allowance after negligent transfer advice
key_facts: Kevin Lennon transferred from the Metropolitan Police Service to the RUC in January 1999 with a break in service caused by his MPS leaving date of 11 January and RUC start date of 31 January.

Mrs Bewley, an MPS personnel officer, handled the transfer and told Lennon his allowances would not be affected by taking time off, but failed to warn that the gap would permanently end his £134.61 monthly housing allowance.
Lennon could not sue for breach of contract because police officers act as Crown servants rather than under contracts of employment.
HHJ Faber awarded £43,810.59 for negligent failure to advise; the Commissioner appealed only on whether a duty of care was owed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court judgment finding the Commissioner liable in negligence for pure economic loss.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; a duty of care arose from an express voluntary assumption of responsibility in the particular transfer transaction.
enrichment.ratio: The Hedley Byrne principle applies to negligent omissions as well as statements where a defendant with special knowledge undertakes a particular task on which the claimant relies; Mrs Bewley's express assumption of responsibility for Lennon's transfer and allowance concerns created a special relationship sufficient to impose a duty to advise, without creating a general employer duty to protect employees from economic loss.
legal_issues: Whether the Commissioner owed a duty of care in respect of pure economic loss from failure to advise on transfer dates
Whether the case created a novel category of liability
Whether the Hedley Byrne principle requires a professional adviser
Whether an employment relationship analogy barred tortious liability

notes: Shelltime 3 charterparty final voyage and off-hire extension issues; detailed maritime construction analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Shelltime 3 final voyage rights after off-hire extension and 15-day margin
key_facts: Kriti Akti was chartered to Petroleo Brasiliero SA on the Shelltime 3 form for 11 months plus 15 days in charterers' option, with a clause 50 extension for off-hire time.
Charterers claimed entitlement to extend the charter to 14 June 2001 by adding 36 off-hire days and the 15-day margin, then ordered a voyage from São Sebastião via Santos to New York.
Owners took back the vessel at Santos, treating the charter as expired and demanding increased hire for any further voyage.
Arbitrators answered the first preliminary question in charterers' favour but the second against them, being bound by The Aspa Maria; Moore-Bick J answered both in charterers' favour.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Moore-Bick J on appeals from an arbitrators' interim final award on two preliminary questions of law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; clause 18 final voyage rights apply to the charter period as extended under clause 50 and include the clause 3 margin period.
enrichment.ratio: Off-hire days added under clause 50 form part of 'the period of this charter' for clause 18 purposes and carry the clause 3 margin; charterers may order a clause 18 voyage commencing during the margin period, and The Aspa Maria does not bind the court to treat the margin as a redelivery tolerance only.
legal_issues: Whether clause 50 off-hire extensions count as part of the charter period for clause 18
Whether the clause 3 '15 days more' margin applies after a clause 50 extension
Whether charterers may commence a final voyage during the margin period
Whether The Aspa Maria governs the construction of the margin in this charter

notes: Undisclosed prosecution witness conviction appeal; safety analysis and supporting evidence are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Undisclosed ABH conviction of prosecution witness in firearm fear appeal
key_facts: McCallan was convicted at Newcastle Crown Court of possessing a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence after an incident at the Top Club where complainant Fortunato alleged a gun was held to his head.
The defence case was that Fortunato gave the appellant a starting pistol for protection because men were looking for him; the appellant did not give evidence.
Fortunato's recent ABH conviction was not disclosed to the defence before trial, though the Crown had told the defence he had no convictions.
The trial judge certified that the conviction might not be safe; supporting evidence included Rennison's account that Fortunato looked shaken and the pistol being found loaded and cocked.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by certificate of the trial judge to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the undisclosed conviction did not render the verdict unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to disclose a prosecution witness's convictions does not inevitably quash a conviction; where the conviction is not for dishonesty, adds little to cross-examination on credit, and the prosecution case is supported by independent evidence including the defendant's failure to give evidence, the verdict remains safe.
legal_issues: Whether non-disclosure of Fortunato's ABH conviction rendered the conviction unsafe
Whether the defence trial strategy would materially have differed
How prior convictions of a crucial prosecution witness affect credibility

notes: First Court of Appeal guidance on protective awards for collective redundancy consultation breaches; comprehensive statutory analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Maximum protective award for failure to consult on factory closure redundancies

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992
Trade Union Reform and Employment Rights Act 1993

key_facts: Susie Radin Ltd closed its Crook factory on 14 July 2000, making 108 employees redundant with GMB recognition.
The employer gave notice on 6 April 2000 but provided no written information required by section 188(4) and conducted no meaningful consultation before dismissal letters were sent on 19 April 2000.
The employment tribunal awarded the maximum 90-day protective period beginning 14 July 2000, estimated to cost about £250,000.
The employer argued consultation would have been futile because closure was inevitable and unfair dismissal claims had failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on the principles governing protective awards under section 189.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the 90-day protective award was not perverse and Talke Fashions compensatory approach should no longer be treated as authoritative.
enrichment.ratio: A protective award is a sanction for breach of mandatory collective consultation under section 188, not compensation for individual loss; tribunals should focus on the seriousness of the employer's default, and where there has been no consultation at all the proper approach is to start with the maximum 90-day period and reduce it only if mitigating circumstances justify doing so.
legal_issues: Whether protective awards are compensatory or punitive
Whether futility of consultation should reduce or eliminate a protective award
What factors tribunals should consider in fixing the protected period
Whether the extended 12-week notice period mitigated the employer's default

enrichment.short_title: War pension dependant allowance refused for post-service cohabitation

statutes_considered.title: Naval, Military and Air Forces Etc. (Disablement and Death) Service Pensions Order 1983

key_facts: Mr Hopkins served in the RAOC from June 1956 to December 1958 and received a war pension and unemployability allowance for pulmonary tuberculosis.

He claimed an additional dependant allowance under Article 18(5) for Ms Newman, with whom he began cohabiting in September 1991, but Schedule 4 required cohabitation to begin six months before service commenced.
The Pensions Appeal Tribunal used the golden rule to read down the requirement to a reasonable cohabitation period; Ms Newman was aged about five when Hopkins began service.
The Secretary of State appealed, contending the SPO is primary legislation and Article 14 ECHR was not engaged.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administrative court appeal by the Secretary of State for Defence against a Pensions Appeal Tribunal decision allowing a dependant allowance claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the PAT decision was quashed and the claim rejected.
enrichment.ratio: The six-month pre-service cohabitation requirement in the SPO was not absurd and could not be rewritten by the PAT; Article 14 requires identification of a recognised ground of discrimination, which was not established on the facts, and Articles 8 and 1 Protocol 1 were not engaged because the benefit is non-contributory welfare provision without a legitimate expectation beyond the statutory terms.
legal_issues: Whether the PAT could reinterpret Schedule 4 using the golden rule to avoid absurdity
Whether Article 14 ECHR requires a personal characteristic or status gateway
Whether the dependant allowance claim fell within the ambit of Articles 8 or 1 Protocol 1
Whether differential treatment of married and unmarried partners was justified

notes: Prison medical correspondence and Article 8 proportionality; exceptional facts and relief are clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Prisoner's confidential medical correspondence under Article 8
key_facts: Szuluk was serving 14 years for drug offences and had undergone brain surgery in 2001, requiring ongoing specialist monitoring every six months.
As a Category B prisoner held in a unit with Category A prisoners, his correspondence was subject to routine reading under PSO 1000 chapter 36.21.
Prison security initially allowed medical correspondence marked 'medical in confidence' without reading, but later required envelopes to be examined by the prison medical officer before resealing.
The claimant argued the medical officer review would inhibit candid correspondence about prison medical treatment for a life-threatening condition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging the prison's revised policy on reading medical correspondence.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the November 2002 decision was not proportionate and the governor was to reconsider in accordance with the judgment's principles; no damages awarded.
enrichment.ratio: Although general prison correspondence rules may justify routine reading for security, Article 8 requires an individual assessment of proportionality; for this prisoner with a life-threatening condition needing confidential specialist correspondence, the initial arrangement allowing marked medical correspondence without content review was proportionate whereas referral to the prison medical officer was not.
legal_issues: Whether routine reading of medical correspondence with external specialists is compatible with Article 8
Whether examination by the prison medical officer was a proportionate interference
Whether exceptional medical circumstances justify departure from PSO 1000
Whether damages were appropriate for the Article 8 breach

notes: Disabled person's tax credit hours calculation; bank holiday trap and regulation construction are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Disabled person's tax credit refused for sub-16-hour average after bank holidays

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992
Disability Living Allowance and Disability Working Allowance Act 1991

key_facts: Simon Taylor, who has learning disabilities, worked 16 hours per week as an assistant gardener under an oral contract negotiated by his father.
His disabled person's tax credit claim of 8 June 2001 was refused because bank holidays reduced his actual hours below a 16-hour weekly average over the preceding five weeks.
He had been off sick with Crohn's disease and underwent major surgery in March and April 2001 before returning to work.
Regulation 6 treated bank holidays differently for current hours under regulation 6(5) than for average hours undertaken under regulation 6(1)(a) and 6(4).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Social Security Commissioner's decision dismissing an appeal from the Inland Revenue refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; selecting a shorter three-week period to avoid the bank holiday effect would have distorted rather than accurately determined average hours.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 6(4)(c)(ii) permits only another preceding period that enables weekly average hours to be determined more accurately; choosing mid-May weeks solely to avoid bank holidays is artificial, and bank holidays are properly disregarded for current-hours tests under regulation 6(5) but not for the average-hours undertaking test under regulation 6(1)(a).
legal_issues: Whether the Inland Revenue was perverse in refusing to use a three-week averaging period
How regulation 6 distinguishes 'engaged' and 'normally engaged' in remunerative work
Why bank holidays are treated differently under regulations 6(1)(a) and 6(5)
Whether the bank holiday trap affects disabled persons tax credit claims
linked_authorities: Linda Case v IRC, 23 January 2002, CTC/3593/2001

confidence.notes: Longmore, Laws, and Peter Gibson LJJ agree on a narrow regulation 6 construction point. Scheme has since moved to working tax credit.

notes: Novel electromagnetic interference nuisance claim; foreseeability analysis and appeal outcome are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Rail electromagnetic interference with recording studio held not foreseeable nuisance
key_facts: Mr Morris operated Soundstar recording studio about 80 metres from the London to Brighton line and lost customers after TI 21 track circuits were installed in October 1994.
Electromagnetic fields from tuned zones interfered with amplified electric guitars, causing unsatisfactory recordings and claimed losses exceeding £60,000.
British Rail's 1991 Bradley report addressed interference to studios under railway arches, not premises at this distance; only one other similar complaint arose among thousands of installations.
The county court held Railtrack liable in nuisance; Railtrack did not dispute that electromagnetic interference could constitute nuisance in principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court judgment finding Railtrack liable in private nuisance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim dismissed because interference at 80 metres was not reasonably foreseeable when the TI 21 system was installed.
enrichment.ratio: Liability in modern private nuisance requires foreseeability of relevant damage as an aspect of reasonableness between neighbours; Bradley's report of minor interference to an under-arch tenant did not make foreseeable harm to a studio 80 metres away, and the abnormal sensitivity rule is subsumed within that broader foreseeability analysis.
legal_issues: Whether electromagnetic interference with electronic equipment can amount to private nuisance
Whether amplified electric guitars in a recording studio are protected ordinary use or abnormally sensitive
Whether Railtrack should have foreseen interference at 80 metres when installing TI 21 circuits
Whether section 122 of the Railways Act 1993 provides a statutory defence
